blocks.text: Every laboratory must have a first aid box. Table 16.1 lists common accidents and their first aid treatments.

blocks.caption: Table 16.1 Accidents and their first aid treatment
rows: Minor cuts
remove any piece of glass; apply a little methylated spirit or tincture of iodine with cotton (both disinfectants)
Serious cuts
apply pressure on the cut for about 10 minutes to stop the bleeding; consult a doctor
Acid in the eye
wash thoroughly with water, then with 1% sodium bicarbonate solution
Alkali in the eye
wash with water, then with 1% boric acid solution
Foreign particle in the eye
do not rub; remove the particle carefully with a soft handkerchief, then wash with water
Soreness in the eye
a drop of olive oil in the eye, kept closed for some time
Burns with dry heat (flame, hot object)
apply burnol or mustard oil
Burns causing blisters
wash freely with ice-cold water, then with saturated sodium bicarbonate solution, then water
Acid burns
wash freely with water, then 1% acetic acid solution, then water; dry the skin and apply burnol
Alkali burns
wash fully with 2% ammonia solution and apply glycerin; wipe off the glycerin after some time and apply burnol
Poison swallowed
spit immediately; wash the mouth with water repeatedly
Acid swallowed
drink a lot of water, or lime water, or milk of magnesia
Caustic alkali swallowed
drink a lot of water; drink a glass of lemon or orange juice
Salt of a heavy metal swallowed
take milk or the white of an egg
Clothes catch fire
do not run; wrap in a blanket or dry cotton cloth; lie down on the floor
Beaker of inflammable liquid catches fire
cover the beaker with a duster or damp cloth to cut off the oxygen supply
Spirit or oil catches fire
throw a mixture of sand and sodium bicarbonate; never water, which spreads the fire
Electrical parts catch fire
switch off the electric supply immediately and throw sand; never water

blocks.alt: Top row: three boxes for physical, chemical and biological hazards with the matching general instructions. Middle: three step boxes for chemical waste, store, label, and transfer and treat. Bottom: a two-column summary of first aid for cuts, eyes, burns, poisons and fire.
blocks.caption: Laboratory hazards, chemical waste disposal and first aid (original diagram after topics 16.1 to 16.4 and Table 16.1).
blocks.long_description: Laboratory hazards are physical, such as wet floors and broken glass, chemical, handled by each chemical's standard procedure and hazard pictograms, and biological, such as allergens and infections from animals. Chemical waste is never poured away: it is stored in proper containers, labelled with the type, date and origin, and taken to an allocated site for neutralization, precipitation, ion exchange, oxidation or reduction. First aid follows Table 16.1: disinfect minor cuts and press on serious ones; wash acid out of the eye with water then dilute sodium bicarbonate, and alkali with water then dilute boric acid; treat burns by washing and the printed dressings; dilute swallowed acid or alkali with water and the printed antidotes; smother burning clothes or liquids and never throw water on burning oil or electrical fires.
